units.translation: Justice inclines to those who have suffered, to learn what is to come.
But no remedy availed to prevent the city from suffering as it now does.
It remains for the doer to suffer.
The doer must suffer; this is the three-times-old saying.
For the doer is also bound to suffer.
The wrath of Zeus, protector of suppliants, remains, hard to appease by the laments of the sufferer.
to suffer evil all one's days
I suffer evil at the hands of Zeus.
To suffer evil at the hands of enemies is not at all unseemly.
having suffered evil, he repaid with evils.
all who, having been well treated, unjustly harm me
I may become (I may be laughed at)
I suffered things hard to bear for the citizens
the clatter of not one spear
Herodotus uses the present πατέομαι [to eat]; the Attic writers use only the aorist ἐπασάμην [I ate] and the future πάσομαι [I will eat].

Thus M, with the gloss γεύσονται [they will taste], one letter having been erased before it, so that it seems to have been σπάσονται [they will draw], which is in several copies, with the note in one γρ. καὶ πάσονται ἤτοι γεύσονται [variant: and they will eat, that is, they will taste], in another γρ. πάσονται ἤγουν φάγωσιν [variant: they will eat, that is, they may eat]. With that compare the adjective λυκοσπάς [wolf-rending].
But the hollow-bellied wolves will not eat his flesh.
What evil, woman, earth-nurtured, edible or drinkable, have you partaken of?
variant: and they will eat, that is, they will taste
variant: they will eat, that is, they may eat
to trample, to hold in contempt
I go to the roof of the house, treading on purple.
Do you boldly tread toward the altar?
to the one who treads on enemies
treading underfoot the glory of the future
for whom the grace of things untouchable may be trodden
For what is not lawful is not to be trodden underfoot with the heel.
And I see all these things trampled underfoot.
Usually said by the tragedians without the article, of men and gods, especially of Zeus, who is often called Ζεὺς πατήρ [Zeus the father], by Homer πατήρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε [father of men and gods].
interpolated writing for τοῦ φόνου [of the murder], about which I have spoken in the annotation.
πατρί [to the father] at the end of the defective verse fr. 229 was supplied by Hermannus.
so that your father may not see you lingering
your father bids you to speak
you seem to say nothing of what your father wants
the father will rend this ravine
the god-hated father of this man, Atreus
the father already has the libations of the dead
so that the father may see
a father or a mother newly suffering might lament these things
the father sends aid from the tomb
a father might come into being without a mother
or does the father err in his counsels?
the father honors those under the wings of Pallas
